mad1-w1-q1.question: A browser opens this URL: `https://shop.example.com:8443/items/list?page=2&sort=price#reviews`. Which part of the URL is **not** sent to the server with the HTTP request?
options: The host `shop.example.com` (which goes in the `Host` header)
mad1-w1-q1.explanation: The fragment (the part after `#`) is only for the browser, for example to scroll to a section of the page; the browser does not include it in the request. The path and query go in the request line (`GET /items/list?page=2&sort=price HTTP/1.1`) and the host goes in the `Host` header, so options A, C and D are wrong. Trap: option A, because people think the query is also browser-only, while the server uses it to filter and sort.

mad1-w1-q2.question: In an app, the `/login` route accepts only GET and POST. A client sends a `DELETE /login` request. Which status code is the most accurate?
mad1-w1-q2.explanation: The resource (`/login`) exists; this method just isn't allowed on it. That is 405, and the response's `Allow` header lists the allowed methods (GET, POST). Option A's trap: the resource was found, so 404 is wrong. Option D (501) is for a server that doesn't recognise the method for any resource at all. Option B (403) is about missing permission, not about the method.

mad1-w1-q3.question: A 2 MB file is downloaded over a 16 Mbps link with an RTT of 80 ms. Before data arrives, 2 RTTs are needed (TCP handshake + request); ignore TLS and server time. 1 MB = 10⁶ bytes, 1 Mbps = 10⁶ bits/s. What is the total time?
mad1-w1-q3.explanation: Latency: 2 × 80 ms = 0.16 s. Transmission: 2 MB = 16 × 10⁶ bits, and 16 × 10⁶ ÷ 16 × 10⁶ = 1.0 s. Total = 0.16 + 1.0 = 1.16 s. Option A's trap: not converting bytes to bits (2 ÷ 16 = 0.125 s, plus 0.16). Option B forgets the latency, and option C counts only 1 RTT.

mad1-w1-q4.question: A browser sends `GET /old-page` and the server replies `301 Moved Permanently` with the header `Location: /new-page`. What happens next?
options: The browser automatically sends a new GET request for `/new-page`, and the address bar shows `/new-page`
The server fetches the content of `/new-page` internally and sends it in the body of that same 301 response
The browser shows the user an error page, because 3xx codes are failures
The browser waits a little and requests `/old-page` again
mad1-w1-q4.explanation: A 3xx redirect means 'the resource is elsewhere': the browser reads the `Location` header and sends a **new request** there, so there are two request-response cycles and the URL changes. Option B's trap: that is like a server-side forward/include, not a redirect; in a redirect the client does the work. Option C is wrong because 3xx is not an error class, and option D is thinking of `Retry-After`/503.

mad1-w1-q5.question: In a fresh browser (no caches) a user opens `https://www.example.org/`. The connection is HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 over TCP. Which order is correct?
options: TCP handshake → DNS lookup → TLS handshake → HTTP request
DNS lookup → TCP handshake → TLS handshake → HTTP request
DNS lookup → TLS handshake → TCP handshake → HTTP request
HTTP request → DNS lookup → TCP handshake → TLS handshake
mad1-w1-q5.explanation: A TCP connection needs an IP address, so DNS comes first. TLS runs on top of TCP, so the TLS handshake comes after TCP. Only once the encrypted channel exists does the HTTP request go out. Option C's trap: putting TLS before TCP because 'security comes first'; but TLS needs a TCP connection to send its bytes. Option A starts TCP without an IP, which isn't possible.

mad1-w1-q6.question: Plain HTTP/1.1 (no TLS), DNS already cached, RTT 50 ms. A browser loads an HTML page that references 5 more files (3 CSS/JS + 2 images, same server). No TCP connection is open yet; the browser opens one **persistent** TCP connection and requests the files one after another (no pipelining). Ignore transmission and server time. What is the minimum time to get all 6 files?
mad1-w1-q6.explanation: TCP handshake = 1 RTT. Then the HTML request-response = 1 RTT, and the other 5 files one after another = 5 RTTs. Total 7 RTTs × 50 ms = 350 ms. Option A's trap: that is the non-persistent connection count, where every file needs a new handshake (6 × 2 × 50 = 600 ms). Option D forgets the handshake (6 × 50), and option B assumes all the files arrived at once.

mad1-w2-q1.question: Which markup is the most accessible for an email input, so that clicking the label focuses the input and a screen reader announces the field's name?
options: `<label>Email</label> <input type="email" name="email">` (label outside the input, no `for`)
mad1-w2-q1.explanation: The label's `for` matches the input's `id`, so the label is programmatically tied to that input: a click focuses it and a screen reader announces the field as 'Email'. Option A's trap: a placeholder disappears as soon as you type and does not replace a label. Option C has a `<label>`, but with no `for` and the input not inside it there is no link; option B's `<span>` is just text.

mad1-w2-q2.question: In this CSS `box-sizing` is not set anywhere (default). What is the card's visible width (from one edge of the border to the other)?
mad1-w2-q2.explanation: With the default `content-box`, `width` is only the content: 300 + 2 × 20 (padding) + 2 × 5 (border) = 350px. Option A's trap: thinking like `border-box`, where 300px would include everything. Option B forgets the border, and option D also adds the margin, but the margin is empty space outside the border, not part of the visible box.

mad1-w2-q3.question: The user presses Go without changing anything. Which URL will the browser request?
options: `/search` (the data goes in the request body)
mad1-w2-q3.explanation: Only controls with a `name` are submitted: `q=flask` and the select's `sort`. A select's value is the chosen option's `value` attribute (`new`), not its visible text (`Newest`). Option B's trap: the `lang` input has only an `id`, no `name`, so it isn't sent. Option C sends the display text, and option D is POST behaviour, while the method here is GET.

mad1-w2-q4.question:
The HTML is `
Home
` and the CSS is below. What colour is the "Home" link?
options: the browser's default link colour, because the rules conflict
mad1-w2-q4.explanation: Specificity: `#menu a` = (1, 0, 1), `nav a.active` = (0, 1, 2), `.link.active` = (0, 2, 0). The comparison goes from the left and only the first rule has an id, so red wins. Option A's trap: 'the last rule wins' or 'two classes are more'; source order only matters when specificity is equal. Option D is wrong because the cascade always resolves a conflict.

mad1-w2-q5.question: The viewport width is first 768px, then 400px. What is the width of `.col` in each case?
mad1-w2-q5.explanation: `max-width: 768px` means width ≤ 768px, so at 768px the first query applies and the width is 100%. At 400px both queries match; specificity is equal, so the later rule (90%) wins. Option A's trap: reading `max-width` as 'strictly less than'. Option B's trap: thinking that after the first matching media query the rest are ignored; in CSS every matching rule enters the cascade.

mad1-w2-q6.question: Two `<div>`s sit one below the other in normal block flow (the parent is a plain block, not flex/grid), with no padding, border or content between them. What is the vertical gap between the border of "One" and the border of "Two"?
mad1-w2-q6.explanation: In normal flow the vertical margins of adjacent block siblings **collapse**: the gap is the larger of the two margins, i.e. max(30, 20) = 30px. Option A's trap: adding the margins as you would horizontally (30 + 20). Collapsing happens only for vertical margins in block flow; margins of flex or grid items don't collapse, and there you would get 50px. Option D's 10px is the difference, which no rule uses.

mad1-w3-q1.question: The context has `courses = ['MAD1', 'DBMS']`. What does this (one-line) template render?
mad1-w3-q1.explanation: In Jinja `loop.index` starts at 1 and goes up on every iteration, so you get `1.MAD1 2.DBMS`. Option B's trap: counting from 0 like Python's `enumerate`; that would be `loop.index0`. Option D assumes the index never increases, and option C has the order reversed.

mad1-w3-q2.question:
A Flask app renders `

{{ comment }}

` in a `comment.html` template, and a user wrote `hi` as the comment. With default settings, what does the browser show?
options: The literal text `hi`, because `<` and `>` were escaped to `<` and `>`
The template fails to render with an error
The `<b>` tags are removed and only a plain 'hi' is shown
mad1-w3-q2.explanation: Flask turns autoescaping on for `.html` templates, so the special characters in `{{ comment }}` become HTML entities and the browser shows them as text, not as tags. Option A's trap: that only happens with `|safe` (and then a `<script>` would run too). Option D is 'sanitizing', which autoescaping does not do; it doesn't strip tags, it turns them into harmless text.

mad1-w3-q3.question: The template is the same both times. First `user = {'name': 'Asha'}` (no `nickname` key) is passed, then `user = {'name': 'Asha', 'nickname': ''}`. What are the two outputs?
options: An error the first time, `Hi !` the second time
mad1-w3-q3.explanation: The first time there is no `nickname` key, so `user.nickname` is undefined and `default` gives 'Guest'. The second time the key exists and its value is an empty string; `default` only acts on undefined values, so the empty string is printed: `Hi !`. Option A's trap: treating `default` like Python's `or`; for that you need `default('Guest', true)`. Option C is wrong because with default settings a missing key does not raise an error.

mad1-w3-q4.question: `base.html` has `<title>{% block title %}Site{% endblock %}</title>`. When the `profile.html` below is rendered, what is the title, and does "Hello" appear on the page?
options: `<title>Profile - Site</title>`, and "Hello" also appears on the page
`<title>Site</title>`, because a parent's block cannot be overridden
mad1-w3-q4.explanation: The child's `title` block replaces the parent's block, and `{{ super() }}` brings back the parent's content 'Site', so the title is `Profile - Site`. In a template that extends another, text outside blocks (here "Hello") is not rendered, because the output is the parent's layout. Option A's trap: treating the child like a normal page where everything is printed. Option B ignores `super()`, and option D gets the meaning of block overriding backwards.

mad1-w3-q5.question: The header has a link ``; there is no text in the link, only a cart icon. What is the best `alt` for the image?
mad1-w3-q5.explanation: Here the image is the link's entire content, so its `alt` becomes the link's accessible name. So the alt should state what the link does: 'View cart'. Option B's trap: `alt=""` is for decorative images that already have text next to them; here it would leave the link without a name and a screen reader would just say 'link'. Option C makes it read a filename that is useless to users, and in option D `title` is not a reliable replacement.

mad1-w3-q6.question: The context has `nums = [3, 4, 7, 8, 10]`. What does this (one-line) template render?
mad1-w3-q6.explanation: `for ... if ...` filters the sequence first, and the `loop` variable counts only the items that enter the loop: 4, 8, 10 get indices 1, 2, 3. Option A's trap: that is what happens with an `{% if %}` inside the loop, where `loop.index` counts positions in the original list (including 3). Option B is like `loop.index0`, and option C reads the condition backwards (odd numbers).

mad1-w4-q1.question: A student can take many courses and a course has many students. What is the correct way to store this in a relational database?
options: A `student_ids` column in the `course` table holding comma-separated ids
A separate association table (such as `enrollment`) with both `student_id` and `course_id` as foreign keys
Merging Student and Course into a single table
mad1-w4-q1.explanation: This is a many-to-many (M:N) relationship, and in the relational model it is represented by an association table in which each row is one (student, course) pair. Option A's trap: one column can hold only one course, which makes it 1:N. Option B allows neither a foreign key nor a join, and option D duplicates data again and again.

mad1-w4-q2.question: In a blog app a User can have many Posts, but every Post has exactly one author. Where should the foreign key go?
options: A `user_id` column in the `posts` table, pointing to `users.id`
Each table holding the other's id
A separate association table is required
mad1-w4-q2.explanation: In a 1:N relationship the FK goes on the 'many' side (posts): every post stores the id of its one author. Option A's trap: a user has many posts, so a single `post_id` column cannot hold them all. Option C creates duplicated and inconsistent data, and option D (an association table) is for M:N, which isn't needed here.

mad1-w4-q3.question: `users` has (1, Asha), (2, Bilal), (3, Chen). `posts` has three rows: two with `user_id = 1` and one with `user_id = 3`. What does this query return?
mad1-w4-q3.explanation: The LEFT JOIN keeps Bilal too, with NULL post columns. `COUNT(p.id)` counts only non-NULL values, so Bilal's count is 0. Option B's trap: thinking like `COUNT(*)`, which would count the NULL row as 1. Option C is the INNER JOIN result, and option D is wrong because COUNT never returns NULL; it returns 0.

mad1-w4-q4.question: Which statement about the model below is correct? (The `User` model's table is `user`.)
options: `author` creates a separate column in the database that stores the user's name
`db.ForeignKey('user.id')` is wrong; it should use the class name `'User.id'`
A Post can be saved without a user, because relationships are optional
In the table the link is only the `user_id` column; `post.author` gives the User object and `user.posts` gives that user's list of posts
mad1-w4-q4.explanation: `relationship` creates no column; it provides Python attributes based on the `user_id` FK, and `backref='posts'` adds the reverse attribute on User. Option A's trap: taking the relationship for a column. Option B is wrong because `ForeignKey` takes a table.column name; the class name belongs in `relationship('User')`. Option C is wrong because `user_id` has `nullable=False`.

mad1-w4-q5.question: A Flask-SQLAlchemy view creates `u = User(email='a@x.in')`, calls `db.session.add(u)`, and returns a response without calling `commit()`. What happens?
options: The row is saved automatically at the end of the request
The row is not saved; at the end of the request the session is removed and the uncommitted work is discarded
The row is saved but appears only after the app restarts
`add()` itself raises an error, because add is not allowed without commit
mad1-w4-q5.explanation: `add()` only marks the object as pending in the session; making it permanent in the database is `commit()`'s job. Flask-SQLAlchemy removes the session at the end of the app context, and a transaction that was never committed is rolled back. Option A's trap: assuming an 'auto-save', which is not the default behaviour. Option D is wrong because calling commit after add is the normal flow; add on its own raises no error.

mad1-w4-q6.question: `User.posts` is a relationship that uses the default (lazy) loading. The database has 50 users. How many SELECT queries does this code run in total?
mad1-w4-q6.explanation: The first query loads all 50 users. With lazy loading, every `u.posts` runs a separate SELECT for that user the first time it is accessed, so 50 more queries: 1 + 50 = 51. This is the **N+1 problem**. Option B's trap: that is the count for eager loading such as `selectinload`, not for the default. Option A assumes a single JOIN like `joinedload`, and option C forgets the first query for the users.

mad1-w5-q1.question: A route is defined with `@app.route('/submit')` (no `methods` argument). An HTML form sends `POST /submit`. What is the status of the response?
mad1-w5-q1.explanation: Without `methods`, a route accepts only GET (plus the automatic HEAD/OPTIONS). The URL matches but the method doesn't, so 405. Option B's trap: thinking 'the request failed, so 404'; 404 is for when no rule matches at all. Option A is wrong because the route existing isn't enough, the method must be allowed too, and option D would happen if an exception occurred inside the view.

mad1-w5-q2.question: `<form action="/signup" method="post">` contains `<input name="email">`. Where does the Flask view find this field's value?
mad1-w5-q2.explanation: A POST form's data is form-encoded in the request body, and Flask exposes it as `request.form`. Option B's trap: `request.args` is only the URL's query string, which a GET form fills. Option C is for a JSON body (for example `fetch` sending `application/json`), and option D is for cookies; a normal form submit puts nothing there.

mad1-w5-q3.question: The route is `@app.route('/user/<int:uid>')` and the view is `def profile(uid):`. What happens for the requests `GET /user/42` and `GET /user/abc`?
options: The view runs for both; in the second case `uid` is the string `'abc'`
`/user/42` works; for `/user/abc`, `int()` fails inside the view and a 500 is returned
For `/user/42`, `uid` is the integer 42; `/user/abc` does not match the route at all, so 404
mad1-w5-q3.explanation: The `int` converter checks during matching: if the segment is digits it passes an int to the view, otherwise the rule doesn't match and, with no other rule, the result is 404. Option C's trap: thinking the conversion happens inside the view and a failure crashes it (500); the view never runs. Option B is wrong because the converter changes the type, and option A ignores the converter.

mad1-w5-q4.question: A POST handler that places an order returns `redirect(url_for('order_status', oid=o.id))` on success instead of `render_template('done.html')`. What is the main benefit?
options: Less server load, because a redirect response is small
If the user refreshes, the browser repeats only a GET, not the form's POST, so no duplicate order is created
HTTP does not allow HTML in the response to a POST
The redirect puts the form data into the URL, which helps debugging
mad1-w5-q4.explanation: This is the Post/Redirect/Get pattern: after the redirect the last request in the browser's history is a GET, so a refresh or back/forward does not POST the order again. Option A's trap: seeing the redirect as an optimisation; it actually costs an extra request. Option C is wrong, a POST response can be HTML; the risk is only a resubmit on refresh. Option D is also wrong, the form data does not go into the redirect URL.

mad1-w5-q5.question: The route `@app.route('/post/<int:post_id>')` has the view function `show_post`. Inside a request, what does `url_for('show_post', post_id=7, ref='mail')` return?
options: An error, because `ref` is not in the route
mad1-w5-q5.explanation: `url_for` fills the rule's variables (`post_id`) into the path, and turns any extra arguments that are not in the rule (`ref`) into the query string. Option B's trap: treating an extra argument as an error; Flask quietly puts it in the query. Option D puts every value in the query and option A puts them in the path; both ignore the rule.

mad1-w5-q6.question: A controller validates a form with this function. What is the output of the code?
mad1-w5-q6.explanation: In the first form `'  '.strip()` is an empty string, so there is a `name` error. `'-5'.isdigit()` is False (the minus sign is not a digit), so `age` = 'number'. In the second form `'075'.isdigit()` is True and `int('075')` = 75, which is outside 18–60, so only `age` = 'range'. Option C's trap: treating '-5' as a number and reaching the range check. Option D treats the leading zero as invalid, and option B ignores `strip()`.

mad1-w6-q1.question: According to HTTP semantics, which of these methods is **not idempotent**?
mad1-w6-q1.explanation: POST usually creates a new item in a collection; send the same request twice and you can get two items, so POST is not idempotent. Option B's trap: PUT also changes data, but PUT sets the whole resource to a given state, so after ten calls the final state is the same. GET (option A) is safe and DELETE (option C) is idempotent: deleting again after a delete changes the state no further.

mad1-w6-q2.question: `POST /api/v1/courses` successfully created a new course. Which status code is the most appropriate for the response?
options: 201 Created, with the new course's URI in the `Location` header
mad1-w6-q2.explanation: 201 Created is the standard when a new resource is created, and the `Location` header tells the client where the new resource lives. Option A's trap: 200 also means 'success', so people send it, but it doesn't signal creation. Option D (202) is for work that has been queued and will happen later, and option C is for a success with no body.

mad1-w6-q3.question: An API needs to read all enrollments of student 17. Which of these endpoints is the most RESTful?
mad1-w6-q3.explanation: Enrollments are a sub-resource of the student, the URI has only nouns, and reading uses GET. Option C's trap: the right URI with the wrong method; POST would create a new enrollment in that collection. Options B and D put a verb ('get', 'fetch') in the URI, which is RPC style; in REST the HTTP method does the verb's job.

mad1-w6-q4.question: A client sends `DELETE /api/v1/items/5` and gets 204. Because of a network glitch the client sends the same request again and now gets 404. Is DELETE still called idempotent?
options: No, because the two response codes were different (204 and 404)
Yes, but only if the server sends 204 both times; sending 404 violates the standard
Yes; idempotence is about the effect on server state, and after both cases item 5 is deleted. The response code may differ
No, DELETE is never idempotent; only GET is
mad1-w6-q4.explanation: Idempotent means the request's effect on server state is the same whether it is sent once or many times. After the first DELETE the item is gone, and after the second the state is unchanged, so DELETE is idempotent. Option A's trap: reading idempotence as 'the same response every time'. Option B is wrong because a 404 the second time is perfectly valid, and option D contradicts DELETE's standard property.

mad1-w6-q5.question: An API view sends this payload as JSON. What is the output of the code?
mad1-w6-q5.explanation: `json.dumps` writes keys in double quotes and turns `True` into JSON's `true` and `None` into `null`; the float 99.5 stays as it is. Option A's trap: that is Python's `print` (repr) of a dict, not JSON; single quotes are not valid JSON. Option B turns booleans/None into strings, and option C writes JavaScript's `undefined`, which isn't a JSON type at all.

mad1-w6-q6.question: In a notes API, note 9 belongs to Meera. Three requests: (i) `DELETE /api/notes/9` with no token; (ii) the same request with Ravi's valid token; (iii) `PUT /api/notes/9` with Meera's valid token and the body `{"title": "x"` (closing brace missing, i.e. invalid JSON). In order, what are the most standard status codes?
mad1-w6-q6.explanation: (i) The client gave no identity at all, so 401 Unauthorized (i.e. unauthenticated). (ii) Ravi is identified but the note isn't his, so 403 Forbidden. (iii) The body can't even be parsed, which is the client's fault: 400 Bad Request. Option A's trap: swapping the meanings of 401 and 403. Some APIs deliberately return 404 in (ii) to hide that the note exists, but option C gives 500 for (iii), which is wrong because bad input is not a server error. Option D swaps (i) and (iii).

mad1-w7-q1.question: Where and how does Flask's default `session` (no extensions) keep its data?
options: In the server's memory; the browser only gets a random session id
In a sessions table in the database
In a browser cookie, signed with `SECRET_KEY` but not encrypted; the user can read the content but cannot change it
In a browser cookie, encrypted; the user cannot even read the content
mad1-w7-q1.explanation: Flask's default session is client-side: the data is serialized into a cookie and signed with `SECRET_KEY`, so a modified cookie is rejected, but the content can be read by decoding it. Option D's trap: confusing 'signed' with 'encrypted'. Options A and B describe server-side sessions, which come from extensions such as Flask-Session, not from the default.

mad1-w7-q2.question: To protect a session cookie from being stolen through XSS, i.e. so that page JavaScript cannot read it via `document.cookie`, which cookie attribute do you set?
mad1-w7-q2.explanation: The browser sends an `HttpOnly` cookie with HTTP requests but hides it from JavaScript, so an injected script cannot steal it. Option A's trap: `Secure` is also a security attribute, but it only ensures the cookie travels over HTTPS; JS can still read it. Option C is about cross-site requests (CSRF), and option D expires (deletes) the cookie immediately.

mad1-w7-q3.question: A WSGI app is called with `environ = {'name': 'Zoë'}`. What is the value of the `Content-Length` header?
mad1-w7-q3.explanation: `'Hi Zoë!'` has 7 characters, but in UTF-8 'ë' takes 2 bytes, so the encoded body is 8 bytes, and `len(body)` counts bytes. `Content-Length` is always in bytes, so this is the correct approach. Option B's trap: counting the string's characters (`len` before encoding). Option C counts the characters of the template `Hi {name}!`, and option D takes 'ë' as 3 bytes.

mad1-w7-q4.question: The response to `GET /logo.png` had `Cache-Control: max-age=600` and `ETag: "v7"`. The user loads the same image again 5 minutes later and then 15 minutes after the first request. The image has not changed on the server. What does the browser do?
options: Downloads the full image from the server both times
Uses the cache both times without contacting the server, because an ETag is present
Sends `If-None-Match` at 5 minutes; downloads the full image at 15 minutes
At 5 minutes uses the cache directly (no server contact); at 15 minutes sends a conditional request with `If-None-Match: "v7"`, and the server replies 304 Not Modified
mad1-w7-q4.explanation: max-age=600 means the copy is fresh for 10 minutes, so at 5 minutes the cache is used without any network. At 15 minutes the copy is stale, but there is an ETag, so the browser asks with `If-None-Match`; the image hasn't changed, so the server sends 304 with no body and the cached copy is reused. Option B's trap: treating the ETag as freshness; an ETag is only for revalidation. Option C reverses freshness and revalidation.

mad1-w7-q5.question: An API uses cache-aside. The cache hit ratio is 0.8. A cache check takes 2 ms; on a miss, after the cache check, the DB query takes another 50 ms. What is the average response time (data fetch only)?
mad1-w7-q5.explanation: Hit: 2 ms. Miss: 2 + 50 = 52 ms (first the cache check, then the DB). Average = 0.8 × 2 + 0.2 × 52 = 1.6 + 10.4 = 12 ms. Option A's trap: forgetting the 2 ms cache check on a miss (0.8 × 2 + 0.2 × 50). Option C swaps the hit and miss probabilities, and option D just takes (2 + 50) ÷ 2, as if both happened equally often.

mad1-w7-q6.question: This Flask app has just started on Gunicorn with 2 sync worker **processes**. Assume requests alternate between the two workers (1st to worker A, 2nd to worker B, 3rd to worker A, ...). After 6 requests to `/hits`, what does the 6th response show?
options: An error, because two processes are changing the same `global` variable
mad1-w7-q6.explanation: Each worker process has its own copy of the module, so `hits` is two separate counters. Worker A handled requests 1, 3, 5 and worker B handled 2, 4, 6; the 6th request is worker B's third, so `hits=3`. Option A's trap: assuming all workers share one memory. Option D is wrong because the processes have separate memory, so there is no conflict at all; that is exactly why a shared counter needs a DB or Redis.

mad1-w8-q1.question: For a comment form, what does **progressive enhancement** correctly mean?
options: Build the whole app in a JavaScript framework and show 'Please enable JavaScript' when JS is off
The form works with a normal POST without JavaScript; when JS is available, enhance the same form with `fetch` so the page doesn't reload
Support only the latest browsers and block older ones
Render all content with JavaScript, because that improves SEO

mad1-w9-q1.question: Riya logs in, opens `/admin/reports` and gets 403 Forbidden, because her role is 'student'. Which check failed?

mad1-w9-q2.question: In a new app, what is the best way to store users' passwords?

A slow password-hashing function (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2 or PBKDF2) with a random per-user salt, storing the salt + hash
Encrypting the password with AES using the server's secret key
mad1-w9-q2.explanation: A salted slow hash is one-way, differs per user and makes every guess expensive. Option B's trap: SHA-256 is a secure hash, but it is far too fast for passwords and, without a salt, equal passwords give equal hashes. mad1-w9-q3.question: What is the output of this code?

mad1-w9-q4.question: A banking app's `/transfer` endpoint identifies the user by a session cookie. Which of these measures does **not on its own** stop a CSRF attack?

mad1-w9-q5.question: Autoescaping is on in a Flask app. Which template line on the comments page opens the way to stored XSS, if `c.text` is a comment written by a user?

mad1-w9-q6.question: The `users` table has three rows: ('asha', '1234'), ('bilal', '0000'), ('chen', '9999'). A vulnerable login builds this query, and an attacker types `x' OR '1'='1` in the username field and `0000` as the pin. What does the query return?

Option A's trap: seeing `'1'='1'` and assuming 'all rows', forgetting precedence. The quotes are balanced, so option D is wrong too. Fix: a parameterized query.

mad1-w10-q1.question: A test opens a headless browser, types an email and password on the login page, clicks Submit, and checks that the user's name appears on the dashboard. What kind of test is this?

mad1-w10-q6.question: This function has only one test: `assert shipping(600, True) == 0`. Which statement about coverage is correct?

mad1-w11-q6.question: An HTTPS site calls `navigator.serviceWorker.register('/static/js/sw.js')` from its `/dashboard` page (no `scope` option, no `Service-Worker-Allowed` header). Which pages will this service worker control?

mad1-w12-q3.question: A server has 4 CPU cores and the number of Gunicorn sync workers is set to (2 × cores) + 1. Each request keeps a worker busy for 200 ms on average (mostly waiting on the DB). Each sync worker handles one request at a time. What is the approximate maximum throughput?

mad1-w12-q6.question: The latencies (ms) of 10 requests to an endpoint are: 80, 85, 90, 95, 100, 105, 110, 120, 130, 2000. Using the nearest-rank method (p-th percentile = the value at rank ⌈p/100 × n⌉ in the sorted list), what are the mean and p90?
mad1-w12-q6.explanation: Sum = 2915, so the mean = 2915 ÷ 10 = 291.5 ms; one 2000 ms request pushed the average to nearly three times the average of the other 9 requests (about 102 ms). p90: rank ⌈0.9 × 10⌉ = 9, and the 9th value is 130 ms. Option C's trap: taking p90 as 'the largest' (here p100/max). Option B uses the median (102.5) instead of the mean, and option D reads the value at rank 8. This is why dashboards show percentiles: 90% of requests finished in 130 ms or less.
